title: "Quickstart"
---

```{python}
#| include: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.style.use("styles/mint.mplstyle")
```

A district has measured under-5 prevalence at 0.45. Pyrethroid resistance in the local
vector population is 0.30, and the nets currently in use are pyrethroid-only at 0.70
coverage. Biting is mostly on humans (`Q0 = 0.85`) and mostly in bed
(`phi_bednets = 0.80`). Transmission is perennial, and there is no spraying.

The next mass distribution is due. The question is what effect switching those nets to
pyrethroid-PBO would have.

## One scenario

A `Scenario` holds one candidate campaign. It describes both the setting as it is now and
the intervention that switches on at the campaign. The seven fields before `eir_target`
give the setting, the `py_*` fields give the current net mix, and the `*_future` fields
give the campaign.

`EirTarget(0.45, "prevalence")` tells `run_scenarios` that 0.45 is a measured prevalence
and not an EIR. It is inverted into a baseline EIR before the emulator sees anything.

```{python}
from estimint import Scenario, EirTarget, run_scenarios

pbo = Scenario(
    name="PBO switch",
    res_use=0.30,          # pyrethroid resistance
    Q0=0.85,               # share of bites taken on humans
    phi=0.80,              # share of bites taken in bed
    seasonal=0.0,          # 0 perennial, 1 strongly seasonal
    irs=0.0,               # current IRS coverage
    eir_target=EirTarget(0.45, "prevalence"),

    py_only=0.70,          # current nets: pyrethroid-only at 70% coverage

    itn_future=0.70,       # the campaign: same coverage...
    net_type_future="pyrethroid_pbo",   # ...different net
)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Future coverage must be set explicitly

`itn_future=0.70` is not "keep the nets you have". Leave it out and both `dn0_future` and
`itn_future` are set to zero, which models the nets being **withdrawn** at the campaign
rather than continuing. The same holds for `irs_future`, which does not inherit `irs`.
Every intervention you want to persist past the campaign must be restated in its
`_future` field, even when nothing about it changes.
:::

## Running a scenario

`run_scenarios` takes a list of scenarios, one here and hundreds later. It converts net
mix and resistance to `dn0`, converts prevalence to a baseline EIR, and then calls the
emulator. It returns one row per scenario.

```{python}
results = run_scenarios([pbo])

results.drop(columns=["prevalence", "cases"]).T
```

Each row of that transposed column is one field of the result. `dn0_use` is the lethality
of the nets in the ground today, and `dn0_future` the lethality of the PBO nets replacing
them. Coverage is unchanged at 0.70, so the switch between the two is the whole
intervention. `eir_baseline` is the transmission intensity implied by a prevalence of
0.45 in this setting, in infectious bites per person per year. `prev_y9` is prevalence at
the campaign, `prev_endline` three years after it, and `cases_endline` the clinical case
rate there.

`hbr_baseline` and `hbr_new` are `NaN`. They are only computed when a prevalence input is
paired with a non-zero `mosquito_delta`. This scenario perturbs nothing about mosquito
density.

## The trajectory

The two columns dropped from the table, `prevalence` and `cases`, are the trajectories.
Each cell holds a 157-element NumPy array rather than a tidy long table.

The grid is 157 windows of 14 days, starting at day 2190, with the campaign at day 3285.
Expressing it as years from the campaign puts zero where the nets change. That gives
three years of pre-campaign baseline, followed by three years of response.

```{python}
import numpy as np

prev = results.loc[0, "prevalence"]

abs_t = 2190 + 14 * np.arange(len(prev))   # day of each 14-day window
years = (abs_t - 3285) / 365               # years from the campaign

print(prev.shape, years[0].round(2), years[-1].round(2))
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Under-5 prevalence for a switch to pyrethroid-PBO nets at 0.70 coverage, in a setting with resistance 0.30 and a measured prevalence of 0.45. The dashed line marks the campaign."
#| fig-alt: "A line chart of prevalence against years from the campaign. Prevalence wanders between about 0.29 and 0.50 over the three years before the campaign and reaches 0.46 at it, then drops sharply to about 0.26 a year after the campaign before climbing back to about 0.47 by the end of the third year."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))

ax.plot(years, prev, color="#00d4aa", lw=2)
ax.axvline(0, color="#8b93a3", ls="--", lw=1, alpha=0.7)

ax.set_xlabel("Years from the campaign")
ax.set_ylabel("Under-5 prevalence")
ax.set_ylim(0, None)

plt.show()
```

Prevalence falls sharply once the PBO nets go out. It reaches its minimum about a year
later, then rises again over the rest of the horizon. The endline value on its own
understates the campaign, since prevalence at three years is well above its minimum at
one.

The three years to the left of the line are not flat. Nor are they expected to be.
`EirTarget` pins prevalence at the campaign, where `prev_y9` is 0.456 against the 0.45
that was measured. What precedes it is the emulator's own history of the setting under
the nets already in place.

Whether PBO is worth the extra cost per net depends on the alternatives. One scenario
cannot say. [Comparing campaigns](../06-scenarios/comparing.qmd) sets five
options against each other in this same district: withdraw, replace like-for-like, PBO,
pyrrole, and PBO plus IRS and LSM.
